chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Chapter 20 says a person often knows in advance which future moments will be hard. They know when distraction tends to win, when avoidance appears, or when an urge usually renegotiates the plan. That is why Eyal introduces precommitments, or pacts, as a way to shape the future moment before it arrives.

A pact is a decision made in advance that changes later behavior. Instead of trusting the future self to improvise perfectly during temptation, the person adds structure ahead of time. The distracting path becomes harder, slower, costlier, or less available, and prior intent gains support.

The chapter matters because it explains why pacts come late in the book. They are not a shortcut around understanding internal triggers, making time for traction, or hacking back external triggers. They work best when those earlier decisions already exist and need protection.

The chapter also keeps an important moral limit. A pact is not punishment theater. It is not cruelty toward the future self. It is honesty about predictable weakness and respect for what the person already decided matters.

That is why the chapter introduces pacts as a category rather than exhausting every subtype at once. Some pacts add effort. Some add explicit cost. Some reinforce identity. The common feature is that they are chosen in advance so the future moment has less power to rewrite the plan.

That prepares Chapter 21 naturally. Once the reader understands why a precommitment works at all, the next step is to study one form of pact that makes distraction more expensive.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Chapter 20 argues that precommitments protect prior intent by shaping future behavior before temptation arrives. A pact is a future-facing constraint chosen ahead of time so the later moment has less freedom to bargain against the plan.

This matters because many weak moments are predictable. The problem is not that the future is unknowable. The problem is that people often wait to solve the problem when the urge is already active. Precommitment changes the environment earlier.

The chapter also explains sequencing. Pacts come after internal triggers, traction, and external-trigger work because they are meant to protect a real plan, not substitute for one. They are support structures, not the whole building.

The chapter avoids turning this into self-punishment. A pact should serve values and prior intent. It should not become a dramatic ritual of proving toughness.

That is why the next chapter can narrow to price pacts. Chapter 20 establishes why future-facing constraints matter at all; Chapter 21 studies one version in detail.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Chapter 20 calls out a common lie people tell themselves: that the future weak moment must be settled live, in real time, with a heroic speech. Eyal rejects that drama. If you already know where the plan tends to crack, why wait for the crack to appear before building support?

A pact is that support. It is a precommitment that changes the future battlefield before temptation arrives. You make the bad path harder, slower, costlier, or less available. You stop asking the future self to perform miracles in a room you could have rearranged yesterday.

This matters because the chapter lands after the earlier methods for a reason. Pacts are not a substitute for knowing your triggers or making time for what matters. They are the lock on a door you have already chosen.

The chapter also refuses punishment theater. The point is not to bully your future self. The point is to be honest that some moments are predictably slippery and deserve architecture, not speeches.

That is why Chapter 21 comes next. Once the category makes sense, the book can zoom in on one pact type that makes betrayal more expensive than it first looks.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Chapter 20 argues that many moments of distraction are foreseeable before they happen. A person often knows which hour, setting, or urge tends to derail the plan. That is why Eyal introduces precommitments, or pacts, as decisions made in advance that shape future behavior before the weak moment arrives.

A pact matters because it changes the future choice environment. Instead of depending on perfect live negotiation, the person makes the distracting path harder, slower, costlier, or less available ahead of time. Prior intent gets structural help rather than a hopeful speech.

The chapter also explains why pacts come late in the book. They are not substitutes for understanding internal triggers, making time for traction, or reducing external triggers. They are supports that protect work already done. A pact without that earlier foundation can become arbitrary or brittle.

The chapter keeps an important moral boundary as well. Precommitment is not self-cruelty. It is not a drama of proving strength. It is an honest admission that some future moments are predictably weak and that values deserve more than last-second improvisation.

That is why the chapter introduces several pact directions without exhausting them. Some add friction or effort. Some add explicit cost. Some reinforce chosen identity. What unites them is the same logic: decide early so the future moment cannot so easily rewrite the plan.

That leads directly into Chapter 21. Once the category is clear, the book can focus on one specific pact type that makes distraction more expensive than it first appears.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Chapter 20 says precommitments protect prior intent by shaping the future choice environment before temptation arrives. A pact is a decision made in advance so the later moment has less room to bargain against the plan.

This matters because the weak moment is often predictable. The person usually knows where distraction tends to win. Waiting to solve it live gives the urge home-field advantage.

The chapter also insists on sequence. Pacts come after internal-trigger work, traction, and external-trigger redesign because they are meant to protect a real plan, not replace one. They are a late-stage support, not an opening move.

The chapter rejects punishment theater. A pact should serve values, honesty, and realism. It should not become a dramatic ritual of making life miserable in the name of discipline.

That is why the next chapter can narrow to price pacts. Chapter 20 teaches the general logic of future-facing constraints; Chapter 21 studies one concrete version.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Chapter 20 names a problem people love to romanticize: they keep waiting for the future weak moment to be solved by better speeches from the same person who already lost there six times. Eyal cuts through that fantasy. If you know where the bridge keeps collapsing, reinforce it before the convoy arrives.

A pact is that reinforcement. It is a precommitment that alters the future battlefield before temptation gets home-field advantage. Make the bad path harder, slower, costlier, or less available. Stop asking the future self to improvise sainthood in a room you could have rearranged yesterday.

This matters because the chapter arrives late for a reason. Pacts are not magic and they are not substitutes for earlier work. They guard a real plan. They are the lock on a door you actually chose.

The chapter also keeps its dignity. This is not self-punishment pageantry. It is architecture born of honesty. Some future moments are slippery enough that values deserve reinforcement, not pep talks.

So Chapter 21 comes next with precision. Once you understand why a pact works, the book can study one version that makes betrayal expensive enough to feel different in the moment.
